blind.description: The interactive seat map is a bare SVG of thousands of `<circle class="seat is-available">` elements with no roles, accessible names, or focusability, so a screen-reader user gets no information about, and cannot select, individual seats.

Ticket listings are marked up as a `role="menu"` with `role="menuitem"` rows (aria-haspopup="dialog") and the actual price/buy element is a `span` with `tabindex="-1"`, so listings are announced as menu commands, Tab reaches only one item, and the purchase control has no button semantics.

The min/max price filter inputs are given the invalid `role="text"` (`<input role="text" aria-label="Minimum price $53">`), stripping their textbox semantics so screen-reader users cannot discover or edit the price filter.

The date picker container is a `div role="menu" tabindex="0"` whose month navigation and every day button are `aria-hidden="true"` and disabled, so it focuses as a single element announced as one concatenated string ("Close CalendarGo back one monthAugust 2026…") with no usable date controls.

Page structure is unhelpful for AT navigation: two identical `

Henry Cho: The Empty Nest Tour

` elements, no `main` landmark, and the ticket list/map sections sit in unlabeled generic divs, making it hard to locate the buying area.

low_vision.description: The viewport meta declares `maximum-scale=1.0, user-scalable=no`, blocking pinch-zoom so magnification users cannot enlarge the dense ticket list, prices, or seat map.

Seat availability/filter state in the map is conveyed only through fill color of 40-unit dots (classes `is-available`/`is-filtered`) with no text, shape, or pattern cue, so low-vision users cannot tell available from unavailable seats.

The event page uses a fixed two-pane desktop layout (`#ismqp-template-left` listings beside `#edp-map-container`) plus a large fixed-viewBox SVG map, which forces two-dimensional scrolling and loses content when magnified/zoomed.

Key controls are tiny icon-only graphics without visible text (1.5em zoom in/out/reset buttons, chevron month arrows, and the unlabeled `rc-slider-handle` price handles), making them hard to see and locate under magnification.

Critical venue accessibility information is visually truncated with an ellipsis inside a button ("…We encourage patrons ..." plus a small "more" affordance), so enlarged text is clipped rather than reflowed and the information is easy to miss.

motor.description: Choosing seats on the map requires pixel-precise clicks on 40-radius `<circle class="seat">` targets packed ~96 units apart, far below minimum target size and unattainable for users with tremor or imprecise pointing.

The price filter is a two-handle `rc-slider` whose handles must be dragged along a shared track (`rc-slider-handle-1`/`-2` at the same rail), a drag-only pointer interaction with no simple click/tap alternative.

The listings are a roving-tabindex `role="menu"` where all but one `menuitem` has `tabindex="-1"` and the price/buy span is `tabindex="-1"`, forcing dozens/hundreds of arrow-key presses to reach a ticket and offering no keyboard path to the buy control.

Panning and zooming the seat map depends on dragging the `.map__zoomer` region (which itself is `tabindex="-1"`) with only small stacked icon buttons as an alternative, so map exploration has no accessible keyboard/click-only equivalent.

Several activation targets are very small and tightly spaced — breadcrumb links, the inline "more" link, the `Filters` button next to the quantity `select`, and the vertically stacked zoom controls — increasing mis-clicks for users with limited dexterity.

frictions.title: Skip to main content link targets missing anchor element
frictions.description: Activating the 'Skip to main content' link repeatedly fails to move focus or viewport because no element with id='main-content' exists in the DOM. VoiceOver remains trapped on the skip link despite dozens of VO-Space activations across sequential attempts (WCAG 2.4.1).

interventions.description: Fix broken skip link by assigning id='main-content' and focusability to the primary content container.

The 'Skip to main content' link on https://www.gov.za/ points to '#main-content', but no element with that id exists in the DOM. When a VoiceOver user activates the skip link, the browser cannot find the target, so focus and the VoiceOver cursor remain on the link. The user repeatedly pressed VO+Space (over 15 times in one segment) expecting to jump past the header, but remained stuck on the skip link and had to manually navigate through every header element. This makes bypassing blocks impossible for keyboard/screen reader users and causes significant lost time and frustration.
interventions.mitigation: Add id="main-content" to the primary content container element on the page, and set tabindex="-1" on that container so it can receive programmatic focus. Ensure the skip link's href is exactly '#main-content' and that activating the link moves keyboard focus and the accessibility cursor to that element. If the main container is dynamic or loaded asynchronously, attach the id to a stable static wrapper. Verify with a screen reader that activating the skip link moves focus into the main content region.

frictions.title: When2meet availability grid lacks accessible grid semantics and cell labels
frictions.description: The interactive availability grid is constructed using unlabelled DIV elements without ARIA table/grid roles, date/time labels, or keyboard focusability, preventing VoiceOver and standard Tab navigation from identifying or interacting with time slots.

interventions.description: Expose the availability calendar as an accessible ARIA grid with labeled focusable time slots.

The availability grid on When2meet is constructed with unlabelled DIV elements and lacks ARIA grid/table semantics, date/time labels, and keyboard focusability. During the observation, VoiceOver could reach axis headers such as time and date labels, but the individual time slots were not announced and could not be activated with VO-Space or standard Tab traversal. As a result, screen reader users and keyboard-only users cannot mark their availability, making the core scheduling interaction inaccessible.
interventions.mitigation: Rebuild or progressively enhance the availability grid with proper ARIA grid semantics: assign role="grid" to the grid container, role="row" to each day/time row container, and role="gridcell" to each individual time slot. Make each slot keyboard focusable with tabindex="0" and add a programmatically computed aria-label that includes the date, time, and current availability state (e.g., 'Friday Aug 14, 9:00 AM, Unavailable'). Add support for activating a focused slot with Space, Enter, or VO-Space, and expose the current availability state to assistive technology using an appropriate state attribute such as aria-pressed or aria-selected. Do not rely on visual color changes alone to communicate the availability state.

Those same slot divs are click/drag targets that are not focusable and expose no button/checkbox semantics, so a screen-reader/keyboard user cannot toggle their availability at all — the page's core task is impossible.

Form controls have no programmatic labels: the Sign In inputs (#name, #password) rely only on adjacent table-cell text, and the time-zone <select> exposes its option list as its name instead of the visible "Your Time Zone:" text.

Who-is-available information is revealed only by mouseover ("Mouseover the Calendar to See Who Is Available") and is written into #AvailableFraction/#AvailableDate/#Available without any live region, so screen-reader users never receive the group results.

The page has no headings, landmarks, or main structure — the event name "Tennis Meetup" and panel titles are plain divs, and content is wrapped in an invalid <http-equiv="pragma"> element — leaving no way to navigate or orient by structure, and <html> also lacks a lang attribute.

low_vision.description: Availability is communicated purely by cell background color (#339900 green vs white/#ffdede) with no text, pattern, or symbol in the slot cells, so users who cannot reliably distinguish the low-contrast fills cannot read the schedule.
The color legends are 30x10 and 100x10 pixel color blocks ("Unavailable"/"Available", #GroupKey gradient) that become meaningless when magnified or when colors are hard to tell apart.
Slot details appear only on hover in the separate #SlotAvailability panel far from the pointer, so a magnified user hovering a cell cannot see the resulting information in the same viewport region.
Fixed-width layout elements (200px legend cells, 100px donation column, 728x90 ad iframe, side-by-side .HalfPanel grids) force two-dimensional scrolling when zoomed to 400%.
Interactive grid slots and the black-background page provide no defined focus or hover outline styling, so a magnification user gets no clear visible indication of the current cell/target.

dhh.description: The embedded third-party Google ad iframes (aswift_0/aswift_1) can play auto-starting media with no page-provided captions, transcript, or audio control, leaving deaf users without access to that content.

motor.description: Setting availability requires a click-and-drag gesture over the calendar ("Click and Drag to Toggle; Saved Immediately") with no single-tap or non-dragging alternative, blocking users who cannot hold and drag precisely.

Individual 15-minute slot divs in #YouGridSlots/#GroupGridSlots are only a few pixels tall and immediately adjacent with no spacing, far below a 24x24 CSS pixel target, causing frequent mis-selection.
The grid offers no keyboard alternative — slot divs are not focusable or activatable via keys — so users relying on keyboard/switch input cannot enter availability.

Group availability details are exposed only through sustained mouseover of tiny calendar cells, with no click-, focus-, or keyboard-triggered equivalent for users with tremor or limited pointer control.
Toggles are saved immediately with no confirmation or undo, so an accidental drag or slip permanently changes the submitted availability data.

interventions.description: Add clear accessible labels to footer social media links.

Footer social media links are announced with uninformative fallback names such as 'link, image, weebly' and 'link, image, posts' instead of the platform name (e.g., Facebook, Twitter). As a result, screen reader users cannot identify the destination or purpose of these links, and repeated navigation across them yields only confusing, non-descriptive announcements.
interventions.mitigation: Give each footer social link an explicit accessible name by adding descriptive aria-label attributes (for example aria-label="Facebook" on the Facebook link, similarly for Twitter, YouTube, Instagram, and Google Plus) and hiding the child svg.social__icon elements with aria-hidden="true". This ensures VoiceOver announces the actual platform name and does not read separate image fragments.

frictions.title: User journey SVG icons focused as empty groups
frictions.description: When stepping sequentially through the user journey section with VoiceOver, four illustrative SVG icons ('Get Going', 'Get Online', 'Get Selling', 'Get Growing') are focused as separate empty groups ('Get Going, empty group'), creating cluttering extra focus stops before reading the actual text titles.

interventions.description: Hide decorative user-journey SVG icons from screen readers.

Four illustrative SVG icons in the user journey section are exposed to VoiceOver as separate empty groups. Each icon receives focus during linear navigation and is announced as 'empty group' (e.g., 'Get Going, empty group') before the actual text title is read. This adds four redundant focus stops, forcing screen reader users to step through purely decorative images to reach meaningful content.
interventions.mitigation: Hide these decorative SVG icons from assistive technology by adding aria-hidden="true" to each .journey-icon svg element (including get-going, get-online, get-selling, and get-growing variants). This will remove the empty-group stops and let VoiceOver go directly to the section titles.

frictions.title: Navigation menu icon announced as empty group
frictions.description: When navigating the main header menu with VoiceOver, a decorative carrot icon inside the 'More' menu item is focused separately and announced as 'Carrot, empty group', creating an uninformative and cluttering navigation stop.

interventions.description: Hide the decorative dropdown carrot icon from screen readers.

This hides the icon from the accessibility tree so VoiceOver announces the 'More' navigation item without the empty-group interruption.

interventions.description: Announce out-of-stock state and notification form appearance via ARIA live region.

When the user selects the sold-out XS size, the page dynamically renders an out-of-stock email notification form and changes the submit button label to 'Sold Out'. No live region announcement or focus movement occurs, so VoiceOver continues reading the radio button and does not inform the user that the selected size is unavailable or that a notification form has appeared. The user remains unaware of this critical status change and cannot discover the form without manually navigating further.
interventions.mitigation: Add an ARIA live region (e.g., role="status" with aria-live="polite") that is populated when a sold-out variant is selected, announcing something like 'This item is out of stock. A notify-me form is available below.' Alternatively, move focus to the out-of-stock container and ensure its content is announced. Verify the announcement works with VoiceOver.

frictions.title: Size radio buttons omit sold-out availability state in VoiceOver
frictions.description: The XS size radio button is visually styled as sold out, but lacks an accessible aria-disabled or sold-out state in the accessibility tree. VoiceOver reads it as a standard option, causing the user to activate an out-of-stock size.

interventions.description: Expose sold-out availability state on size radio buttons for screen readers.

The XS size option is visually styled as sold out (wrapper class 'sold-out'), but the radio input does not expose an accessible disabled or sold-out state. VoiceOver announces it as an ordinary selectable option, so the user activates it expecting to select the size. This leads to a failed selection and the user must later discover the out-of-stock condition through unannounced page changes.
interventions.mitigation: Expose the sold-out state on the size radio input itself, for example by setting aria-disabled="true" on the input and adding 'Sold Out' to its accessible label, so assistive technologies announce the unavailability before activation. Ensure the visual sold-out styling matches the programmatic state.

blind.description: The three warning/watch/advisory map images (`img#us`, `img#alaska`, `img#hawaii`) have no alt attribute and the active alert status they show is conveyed only by map colors, so a screen-reader user gets no text equivalent of the page's core hazard information (the instruction "Click on the map above for detailed alerts" is also pointer-dependent).
The `<html>` element has no lang attribute, so screen readers may announce the whole page (including alert wording like "Flash Flooding Threats") with the wrong speech synthesizer.

Form fields are exposed with no accessible name (the accessibility tree shows `input#inputstring`, `#query` and `#myfcst-location-input` as unnamed textboxes) and use fake placeholders as real values (`value="Enter location ..."`, `value="City, ST"`), so users cannot tell what to type or that stale text must be deleted.

There are no landmarks, no skip link and no headings other than the single news `h1`, while the page contains several hundred `<area>` links inside the US image map, forcing sequential traversal of the entire map to reach page content.

The exit-warning overlay (`div#nwsexit-warning-dialog`) is plain divs with `href="#"` "Continue/New Window/Cancel" links and no dialog role, name or focus management, so its text is read as stray page content and its controls give no state or purpose to assistive technology.

low_vision.description: The alert map is a fixed 800x500 raster PNG with embedded state/office text; magnifying it pixelates the labels and forces two-dimensional panning to find one's own region, with no scalable text equivalent.

Alert severity/type is communicated purely by color, both on the map PNG and in the legend's empty color swatches (`div.wwabox` containing only ` `), so users who cannot distinguish or resolve the small color chips cannot map a color to "Tornado Warning" etc.

Top-navigation submenus (`div.sub` under FORECAST, INFORMATION, ABOUT, SEARCH) appear only on hover and vanish when the pointer leaves, making them very hard to keep visible while zoomed and offering no way to dismiss or hover over the revealed content reliably.

The legend is laid out in four fixed side-by-side columns (`#wwaleft`, `#wwacenter_l`, `#wwacenter_r`, `#wwaright`) in a fixed-width template, so at high zoom the alert list requires horizontal scrolling and its reading order becomes hard to follow.

Interactive text is very small and tightly packed (legend links, `#territorylinks`, footer link stacks) and the search fields display grey pseudo-placeholder values as real content, reducing legibility of essential controls when enlarged.

motor.description: The primary way to reach local alerts is the image map, whose targets include areas only a few pixels across (e.g. `<area shape="circle" coords="115,302, 3">`, `coords="109,291, 2"`) and sliver polygons, demanding pointer precision most motor-impaired users cannot achieve.

Main navigation submenus are exposed only while hovering the parent item (`div.topMenuNavList` + adjacent `div.sub`), requiring the pointer to be held steady and dragged along a narrow path to reach items like "Rivers and Lakes".
Link lists are densely stacked with minimal spacing (the four legend columns, `#territorylinks`, the social-media row, and the two footer link columns), so adjacent links are easily mis-clicked.
The "Location Help" control is a `javascript:void(window.open(...))` link that spawns a fixed 530x500 popup window, forcing extra window management and giving no in-page alternative.

Both search fields ship with dummy text in their `value` attributes ("Enter location ...", "City, ST") that must be manually selected and deleted before typing, adding avoidable precision input effort to the only text-based alternative to the map.

frictions.description: The weather.gov webpage lacks ARIA landmark roles or semantic structural HTML tags, causing VoiceOver's Rotor Landmarks menu to announce 'No items in Landmarks menu' when activated, blocking structural navigation (WCAG 1.3.1, 2.4.1).

interventions.description: Inject ARIA landmark roles into header, navigation, main content, search forms, and footer elements so VoiceOver Rotor landmark navigation works.

The weather.gov page uses generic container elements for major sections (header, top navigation, main content, and footer) without ARIA landmark roles or equivalent semantic HTML structure. When the user opened the VoiceOver Rotor and selected Landmarks, VoiceOver announced 'No items in Landmarks menu'. Consequently, a VoiceOver user cannot jump directly to main content, navigation, search, or footer regions and is forced to traverse the page linearly, which is time-consuming and disorienting on a content-heavy site.

Ensure these landmarks are present after dynamic updates so VoiceOver Rotor landmark navigation is always available.

frictions.title: Uber Eats item customization dialog requires wide viewport panning under magnification
frictions.description: The item modal layout places option labels and selection controls across wide rows, forcing repetitive horizontal panning under macOS Zoom to read option names and locate controls.

interventions.description: Compact item customization modal layout to keep option names and controls close together for magnified viewports.

The item customization modal lays out flavor labels and stepper controls across wide rows. blind.description: The store's category navigation links (e.g. "Featured items", "Deals") have hrefs that are bare UUID strings (href="0379a62a-1156-4ddb-a09a-7e1dc45d5dfb") rather than in-page fragment anchors, so a screen-reader user activating them is taken to a non-existent relative URL instead of jumping to the menu section.

A modal container is exposed with role="dialog" and the accessible name "dialog" (no aria-label/labelledby heading), so a screen-reader user landing in it hears no purpose and cannot tell what is being asked or how to dismiss it.

The Delivery/Pickup switcher is built from bare <div role="radio" aria-checked> elements with no wrapping role="radiogroup" or group label, so the options are announced as isolated radios with no indication of the set or of what changes when toggled.

Rating and popularity data is conveyed by icon-only SVGs with stray visually hidden filler text, e.g. the store rating renders as "4.3" + hidden "x" + <title>Star</title> and item cards read "$13.19 • 73% (175)" with an unlabelled thumbs-up path, so the meaning of the numbers is lost or garbled.

Document structure is misused — a second <h1> is used for the numeric rating "4.3" while menu sections are <h3>, and carousels nest <ul> directly inside <ul> — breaking heading and list navigation for screen-reader users scanning the long menu.

low_vision.description: The viewport meta tag sets "maximum-scale=2.0", capping pinch-zoom at 200% so low-vision users cannot magnify the dense menu text further on touch devices.

Item names, prices and descriptions sit in line-clamped/truncated containers (classes _ln _lo _lp, _v3 with fixed card widths), so enlarging text or zooming clips the item description and rating text rather than reflowing it.

Featured-item content is presented in horizontally scrolling carousels next to a sticky vertical category nav (#store-desktop-vertical-menu-nav) and sticky header, forcing both vertical and horizontal scrolling and consuming most of the viewport at high magnification.

Primary actions are tiny icon-only glyphs with no visible text label — the 20px "Quick Add" plus overlaid on each food photo, the 16px "View more options" three-dot button, and 12–16px info circles — making them hard to locate and identify under magnification.

The in-store search field has no visible persistent label (only the placeholder "Search in Wingstop (3500 Washtenaw Road Suite F)" and an empty name attribute), so the field's purpose disappears once text is entered and the low-contrast placeholder is the only cue.

motor.description: Interactive controls are very small and tightly packed — 20px "Quick Add" buttons overlaid on the corner of each item image inside the card link, 16px three-dot "View more options", and adjacent Previous/Next carousel arrows separated by a 4px spacer — inviting mis-taps that add an item or navigate unintentionally.

The Delivery/Pickup selector uses generic <div role="radio" tabindex="0"> elements rather than real radio inputs, so keyboard-only users have no arrow-key or reliable Enter/Space activation path for changing dining mode.

Because the menu category links resolve to invalid relative UUID URLs instead of section anchors, keyboard users have no working bypass and must tab through hundreds of item links and Quick Add buttons to reach a later menu section.

Featured-item rows are horizontal scroll containers (nested lists inside overflow carousels) whose off-screen items generally require dragging/lateral scrolling, and the provided Previous arrow starts in a disabled state, offering limited single-pointer alternatives.

interventions.description: Stack flight result row details vertically into a compact column to fit magnified viewports.

blind.description: The banner contains an empty top-level heading (`<span role="heading" aria-level="1">` with no text) while the real page heading "Flight search" (class HeMQ4) is visually hidden, so heading-based navigation lands on a blank "heading level 1" and gives no orientation.

The date picker exposes day cells as `role="gridcell"` wrapping inner `role="button" tabindex="-1"` elements, with weekday header row and many cells marked `aria-hidden="true"` and no grid accessible name, so screen-reader users cannot reliably read or choose a departure/return date.

The "Loading results" progressbars (`role="progressbar" aria-label="Loading results" aria-hidden="true"`) are hidden from AT, so the asynchronous fetching and arrival of the 23 flight results is not announced.

The ticket-type and cabin-class widgets are custom comboboxes whose `aria-controls` points at an empty `aria-hidden="true"` listbox (ids i9 / i22) while the real options live in a separate `ul`, and the combobox itself carries `aria-live="polite"`, producing wrong or duplicated announcements of the available/selected values.

Primary navigation is built from `<button ... role="link">` items (Explore, Flights, Hotels) and duplicated in the drawer as `div role="link" tabindex="0"` with labels like "Selected Tab: Flights", giving conflicting role/state semantics and a second, redundant navigation set to screen-reader users.

low_vision.description: The viewport meta sets `maximum-scale=1.0, user-scalable=no`, preventing pinch/browser zoom of the flight search UI on touch devices.
The date-picker dialog renders several full month grids (July–October…) side by side in a fixed-width scrolling panel, forcing both horizontal and vertical scrolling once magnified.

Icon-only controls (swap origin/destination, add multiple airports, change appearance, calendar month chevrons) convey their purpose only through hover-triggered tooltips (`EY8ABd-OWXEXe-TAWMXe`, `aria-hidden="true"` until hover) that a magnifier user may never see or that disappear on pointer movement.

Calendar state such as the chosen departure day is signalled only by background/color styling classes (e.g. `Ic3tg NXzzqb g7lVZ` on August 18), with no visible non-color indicator, making the selection hard to spot when zoomed or in low contrast.

Key controls use very small glyphs and dense text (16–18px SVG stepper and remove icons, single-letter weekday headers, tiny "Aged 2-11" secondary labels), which pixelate/clip badly under screen magnification.

motor.description: Selecting travel dates requires hitting tiny, tightly packed day cells in the month grids (`div.WhDFk` gridcells), whose inner activatable `role="button"` is `tabindex="-1"`, so imprecise pointer users have no reliably large target or simple tab-stop alternative.

The calendar's month/step chevron buttons are `tabindex="-1" aria-hidden="true"` inside containers wired to `mousedown`/hover handlers, so they are effectively pointer-hover-only with no keyboard-operable equivalent.

Passenger counts must be set by repeatedly clicking 16px `+`/`−` icon buttons ("Add adult", "Remove infant on lap") that sit immediately next to each other, demanding repeated precise clicks with no direct numeric entry.

Origin/destination chips place a small `role="button"` "Remove" control (16px X icon) inside the selected `role="option"` item, so a slightly off-target click deletes the chosen city instead of selecting it.

Several essential controls are non-native `div role="button"/role="link" tabindex="0"` (Main menu, Google apps, drawer items), relying entirely on scripted key handling, so keyboard-only or switch users may be unable to activate them with Enter/Space.

frictions.title: Cart item remove button hit target is undersized
frictions.description: The cart item removal icon ('x') has a small target bounding area (~12x12 CSS px), causing pointer alignment hesitation and multiple click attempts when operating under magnification. (WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size)

interventions.description: Enlarge the clickable hit area of the cart item removal buttons.

The cart item removal icon is only about 12x12 CSS pixels in clickable area. Under macOS Zoom, the user had to carefully align the cursor over this tiny target and made multiple click attempts before the item was removed. Small interactive targets become disproportionately harder to hit when the pointer movement is magnified, causing friction and increasing the chance of accidental clicks on neighboring elements.
interventions.mitigation: Increase the hit area of the remove button to at least 24x24 CSS pixels, with 36x36 recommended. For the '.x-item' anchor elements inside '.li-cart', apply 'display: inline-flex; min-width: 36px; min-height: 36px; align-items: center; justify-content: center; padding: 6px;'. This enlarges the interactive bounding box while keeping the visual icon unchanged, making the control easier to click for magnified pointer users.

frictions.title: Cart item controls widely separated forcing excessive horizontal panning
frictions.description: Item titles and quantities are placed on the far left while remove buttons and prices are on the far right, requiring continuous horizontal panning across empty whitespace under screen magnification. (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow)

interventions.description: Position remove buttons and prices closer to item titles in cart rows.

In each cart row, the item title and quantity are aligned to the far left while the remove button and price are aligned to the far right using a wide flex layout. When the user magnifies the page, only a narrow horizontal slice of the row is visible at a time, so related controls are never on screen together. Concretely, target the '.flex-apart' container within '.li-cart' and change its justify-content to 'start' with a gap of about 16px. This ensures that all controls for an item share the same magnified viewport, reducing the need for horizontal panning.

The embedded keynote video presents spoken presentation content without an author-provided closed caption track or a CC toggle in the player. The user therefore had to rely on macOS Live Captions, an automated speech-to-text fallback, to access the spoken content. This creates a barrier for people who are deaf or hard of hearing because they cannot get synchronized, accurate captions from the media itself, and automated captions are not a reliable equivalent for authored captions. If a separate transcript is already available in the page, it can supplement the captions, but it should not replace the need for synchronized captions on the video itself.

blind.description: The 90-minute keynote is delivered only as a <video> element with an mp4 source and no transcript, descriptive text, or audio description, so blind users get no equivalent for the visual product demos.

Several interactive controls have no accessible name — the video overlay button (`button.Video__overlay`) and the mobile menu close button both expose as "button" with name null in the accessibility tree — so users cannot tell what activating them does.

Heading structure is meaningless: multiple h1s exist (the Stripe logo h1, nav group titles like "Payments"/"Revenue", and the metadata labels "Keynote" and "Runtime" marked as Copy__title h1) alongside the real page title, so heading navigation cannot be used to orient.

The muted keynote clip has autoplay and loop set and begins playing immediately with no programmatically exposed pause/stop before it, so the screen reader user lands in continuously changing media they must hunt for controls to stop.

There is no skip link before the banner, and the mega-menu/mobile-menu panels are aria-hidden with every link given tabindex="-1", forcing sequential traversal of a huge header while the product navigation itself may be unreachable by keyboard/screen reader.

low_vision.description: An autoplaying, looping ambient video sits directly behind the gate CTA and form, and there is no visible pause control before it, so constant motion under magnification makes reading the surrounding text and form very difficult.

Decorative and functional icons are tiny (7×7 px nav carets, 10×8 px hover arrows, 16×16 px hamburger/close icons) and rely on thin strokes, so their state and meaning are lost or blurry when enlarged.

Breadcrumb and CTA rows are wrapped in HorizontalOverflowContainer tracks (one explicitly disabled on mobile), producing horizontally scrolling regions that break reflow and hide the "Register for Sessions 2027" link at high zoom.

Supporting copy such as the SessionsBanner "text-subdued" description and the GatedVideo__playButtonDescription ("Complete form to watch full video") is rendered in low-emphasis small grey text, risking insufficient contrast for critical gating instructions.
The sticky site header (SiteHeader__stickyContainer) remains fixed over the content, consuming a large share of the magnified viewport and obscuring the video and form while scrolling.

dhh.description: The keynote video element contains only a <source> mp4 with no <track kind="captions">, so all spoken content of the 01:30:01 keynote and the preview clip is inaccessible to deaf users.
No transcript or text summary of the keynote is provided on the page beyond a one-line description, leaving no alternative route to the spoken content.

There is no visible caption toggle or statement of caption availability near the "Watch preview" gate, so a deaf user must submit a lead-generation form before discovering the media may be uncaptioned.

motor.description: Header navigation panels are hover/pointer-driven and are rendered aria-hidden with all their links set to tabindex="-1", so users who cannot hold a precise hover or who rely on keyboard cannot reliably open and select items in the Products/Solutions menus.

Many controls are far smaller than 24×24 CSS px and tightly packed — the 7×7 px nav caret buttons, 10×8 px hover arrows, and the 16×16 px hamburger/close/back buttons in the mobile menu — making accurate clicking hard for users with tremor.
Seeking within the 90-minute video depends on the native progress bar, a thin drag-based slider with no single-pointer alternative such as skip-forward/back buttons.
The autoplaying looping preview video starts without user action and offers no easily reachable pause affordance, forcing extra precise pointer work to stop unwanted playback.

The gated form (Form__form with novalidate and many hidden fields) must be completed to reach the full video, and long multi-field input with no visible progressive save increases physical effort and error cost for motor-impaired users.
